issues.evidence: probe p23: a scheduler.json with a<->b cycle makes report print an empty 'Execution order:' and exit 0
issues.summary: load() does not check the persisted graph for cycles or unknown dependencies, so report silently leaves out jobs that are in a cycle.

issues.evidence: probe p22: priority "x" in scheduler.json -> TypeError traceback at A/scheduler.py:85
issues.summary: load() checks that each field exists but not its type, so a hand-edited state file can crash commands with a traceback.
Code is clean but uses old-style formatting and has many lint findings.

issues.evidence: static/B-ruff.txt: C901 load (18) and add_job (12) complexity
issues.summary: load() and add_job() are long, branchy functions.
Priority is optional with a default of 5 that the task did not ask for; jobs added after a dependency failed are auto-cancelled, which goes further than the spec (reasonable).

blinding_guess.why: Both are similar idiomatic single-file implementations; A ships a test suite but neither shows clear signs of a spec framework.

notes: Both sides pass all 21 core behavioural probes (validation, order, run-next, failure propagation, ready never persisted, recompute on load). The only differences are with hand-edited or corrupted state files: B validates the whole graph on load, while A can crash or silently drop jobs that form a cycle. Cycle-on-add (R8) cannot be triggered through the CLI alone, so probe p08 seeds a state file; both reject the add, B because the seeded file has an unknown dependency. A has 8 passing subprocess tests; B has no tests. Bandit reports only low findings in A's tests; no security issues in either scheduler.
